opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, that's a good question, and it gets at what we were actually trying to measure.

When we built CORE-Bench, we drew on papers whose code had already been shown to run successfully on CodeOcean. So we knew, as a ground truth, that the code *can* reproduce the reported results given the right environment. That's the key point: reproducibility is a property of whether the results can be regenerated from the artifacts, not of whether every convenience file comes neatly packaged.

In the harder versions of the task, the agent doesn't get the full environment handed to it. It has to figure out the dependencies, install the right libraries, sometimes deal with version issues, find the right entry point, and then run things. That's deliberate, because it mirrors what a real researcher faces. If you've ever tried to reproduce someone's paper, you know the README is often incomplete, there's no requirements file, or it's pinned to versions that no longer install cleanly. A competent human can usually still get it working with some effort. So we'd say the code is reproducible in the sense that a skilled person could do it, and the question is whether an agent can do that same work.

If we'd only included papers with pristine setup, we'd be measuring something much easier and frankly much less useful. The value of an agent here is precisely in handling that messy, under-specified middle ground. And we found that's exactly where agents struggled. They could often do the easier version where the environment was given, but performance dropped a lot when they had to reconstruct the setup themselves.

So missing setup files aren't a sign the code is irreproducible. They're the realistic friction that makes reproduction hard, and that's what we wanted the benchmark to capture.

r001.rationale: The response says a skilled person can infer dependencies, install libraries, resolve version issues, and find the entry point despite missing setup files, so the code can still be reproducible.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so that was a deliberate choice, and it took some thinking. When we built CORE-Bench, the thing we were trying to measure was computational reproducibility, which is a narrower notion than people sometimes assume. It's not "does the science hold up," it's "given the code and data the authors released, can you re-run it and get the results that are in the paper." And a lot of the papers we looked at, which are all drawn from Code Ocean capsules, had the core scientific code there, the data was there, but the environment setup was incomplete. Missing requirements files, undeclared dependencies, maybe a shell script that assumed some package was already installed.

Our view was that this is actually the realistic state of scientific code, and if you only counted papers that had a perfect one-click setup, you'd be filtering down to a tiny, unrepresentative slice. The whole reason we wanted a benchmark for agents is that this is the messy middle where a human grad student spends a day figuring out what version of some library the authors must have used. So we treated a paper as reproducible if a person with reasonable expertise could, in principle, get it running and recover the reported results, and we verified that ourselves for every task in the benchmark. If we couldn't get it to work, it didn't go in.

So the missing setup is sort of the point. It's part of what the agent has to solve. The three difficulty levels reflect that: the easy level hands you the outputs already, the medium level gives you a working environment and a Dockerfile, and the hard level is the raw repository where the agent has to figure out installation and dependencies on its own. Those hard tasks are where you see the biggest drop-off in agent performance, and I think that's the honest signal about where these systems actually are. If you'd scrubbed all that friction away, you'd be measuring something much easier than the real problem.

r001.rationale: The response says a person with reasonable expertise can infer dependencies and other missing setup details, get the code running, and recover the reported results.

astra-6.text:
The distinction is between reproducibility and ease of reproduction. A missing setup file makes it harder to run the code, but it doesn’t necessarily mean you can’t reproduce the result. You may still be able to identify the dependencies, reconstruct the environment, and get the expected output.

That setup work is part of the challenge in CORE-Bench. We’re not assuming the repository runs out of the box; we’re asking whether an agent can do the work needed to reproduce the result. Of course, if essential information is missing and the result can’t be recovered, that’s a different situation.

r001.rationale: The response says missing setup files can be overcome by identifying dependencies and reconstructing the environment, describing that setup work as part of what an agent does to reproduce the result.

sol-6.1.text: We distinguish between whether the authors have fully documented the environment and whether someone can reproduce the results. Missing setup files certainly make the task harder, but they don’t necessarily make it impossible. You may be able to infer the dependencies from the code, get it running, and recover the expected results. In CORE-Bench, that successful execution is what matters. We’re testing whether an agent can bridge those gaps, rather than treating the presence of a setup file as proof of reproducibility.

r001.rationale: The response says someone can infer dependencies from the code and get it running despite missing setup files, identifying that ability to bridge setup gaps as why the code can still be reproducible.
